slides.title: Product Laws of Exponents
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the prerequisite: a rational base is squared by squaring numerator and denominator. A board showing 4/3 or 2/9 tells you the base was not treated as one number.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Students copy the three vocabulary rows. Say them aloud: base, exponent, power. The exponent COUNTS factors; it is not a factor itself — that is the misconception behind 2³ = 6.
OFF: Ask: what does 2 to the 3 mean? Insist on the answer 'three 2s multiplied', not 'six'.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Expand both powers, count the factors, then write the rule. The law only applies when the bases match: 3²·2³ has no shortcut, and the reveal on the second row is the reason.
OFF: 'We are not adding the bases and not multiplying the exponents. We are counting factors.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Expand (2·5)³ as three copies of (2·5), regroup with the commutative and associative properties, and read off 2³·5³. The trap is a SUM inside the parentheses: (10 + (−2))³ is 8³, and the exponent does not distribute over addition. Question 9 of the round tests exactly this.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
(4²)³ is three copies of 4², so six 4s: multiply the exponents. Then the identity law: one factor of the base is the base. Students who write 4² · 3 = 12 or 4⁵ (adding) are confusing this with the product law; the reveal on the table makes the count visible.
OFF: 'Product of powers: add. Power of a power: multiply. Both come from counting factors, so count if you forget.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: Two ways to the same value.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Read the expression, ask which law applies and why (same base). Do not write yet.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Left column: the law, one exponent, then the value. Right column: evaluate each power and multiply. Same 243 either way — that is the check students can always run.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a student who multiplied the exponents (2¹² = 4096) or multiplied the bases (4⁷). A board reading 128 or 2⁷ is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: A negative base and a power of a power.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The brackets are not absolute value bars — say so before anyone asks. Ask: how many factors of (−2) are there in total?

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Multiply the exponents: six factors of −2. An even number of negative factors gives a positive product; the sign question is the one students carry into Lesson 3.02.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches the added-exponent error ((−3)⁵ = −243, a negative answer) and the dropped sign (a student who writes 3⁶ gets 729 too — ask them to write the base with its sign).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.note: Rational base. This is the B1G-M example item for 7.NSO.1.1. A board with 1/10 multiplied the bases' denominators by the count; 1/6 multiplied exponents and used ½ once.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written. The law needs a product; a sum is evaluated first. Accept any answer that says 'add first' and lands on 512. A student who writes 10³ + (−2)³ = 992 has distributed the exponent over addition — the misconception this question exists to surface.
